standfirst: The strongest El Niño yet measured is being managed, for now, by the institutions that forecast it rather than by the ones that would have to respond: a famine early-warning system put the whole 2026–27 event on the record in one global report, and the Horn of Africa's famine risk changed its driver from drought to flood without changing magnitude. In the same week the presidency of November's climate conference answered a finance shortfall by reaching into the defence budget — "what does it mean to spend 5% for defense if you don't have a country to live on?" — while a draft of the European Union's own negotiating position said there is no scope for new climate finance at all.
orientation:
Claims carry one of three marks. **Evidence** is what the sources actually support. **Contested** is where researchers or practitioners genuinely disagree. **Framing** is advocacy, policy narrative or institutional positioning. **Gap** is a verified absence — something looked for and not found. Sections A and D do not use the marks: A is curriculum reading, D is attributed action.

Two arguments run through this week and they pull against each other.

The first is about lead time, and it is the better news. Every technical precondition the field has spent twenty years asking for is now present at once. The seasonal forecast is about as confident as seasonal forecasts get. The basins at risk are named. The measures are specified. The classification systems have published their scenarios months ahead. B1 and B2 are what that looks like: an early-warning institution saying, in October, which lean season in early 2027 will be the bad one, and why. The field calls this anticipatory action and treats it as its central operational doctrine. What this week does not show is any instrument whose calendar has moved to match. B6 is the same clock from the other end — a sovereign request for an emergency decision, six weeks old, against a board that has never granted one and may not meet before November.

The second is about register, and it has reversed. For two months this digest has recorded climate arguments being made in whichever security language was locally available — energy supply, economic security, resilience — because the field's own vocabulary was unavailable in the room. This week the traffic ran the other way. A climate conference presidency reached for the alliance's defence-spending commitment to price its finance ask (D2), and a foreign minister told a security audience that climate impacts are being **used as a weapon** (B5), which names an adversary where this field's own term, threat multiplier, names only a condition. Read B5 against A1: the Copenhagen framework that section A takes up this week exists to describe exactly that move, and to ask what it buys and from whom.

One correction runs underneath both, and it is this publication's own. The fight over the reference science is not about which body certifies. It is about when the certificate arrives. See B4 and the pushback.
housekeeping:
**What could not be read this week, and what it costs.** The climate panel's own media advisory refused retrieval, so the dates and venue of its plenary rest on the advisory's title and on April reporting that announced the same week and city; the two agree, and the agenda itself is therefore reported rather than read, which matters for B4 because an agenda is where a deferral is arranged. The newspaper carrying the November presidency's remarks on defence spending is paywalled; the quotations in D2 come from a secondary rendering of the same wire report and should be checked against the original before anyone quotes them in print. The Council of the European Union's forward look would not open, so the October meeting schedule in C rests on a quoted listing. A carbon-market trade service carrying the latest date for the European resilience framework would not open. The journal page for this week's recent reading refused retrieval, so section A's second item rests on its abstract. The curriculum reading itself — a 1998 book, in copyright — could not be opened at all, and section A says so and quotes nothing from it.

**Figures dropped rather than hedged.** A reconstruction requirement for the Nepali flood of about US$3.6 billion, which appears in commentary and in no government document. An emergency recovery allocation of 4.1 billion baht for the Thai floods, which appears in one secondary report. A claim that 36 million people have been pushed into acute hunger by this El Niño, which conflicts with the agencies' own 49 million and comes from neither of them. A dollar conversion of the British pledge to the Pacific fund, which two Fijian outlets give almost a hundred per cent apart; only the sterling figure is stated.

**One correction to the published record, and it is this digest's own framing rather than a fact.** Last week's digest opened a question about whether the climate panel remains the reference science for climate decisions, and framed it around states wanting other scientific bodies to guide them. That is not what is being contested. The pushback sets out what is, and why the version that is actually happening is worse. Two smaller corrections, both to this digest's standing notes rather than to anything a reader has seen: the July analysis of the Dutch defence climate strategy is by the director of the Hague centre's climate, water and food security programme and is dated 15 July, not by another researcher on the 16th; and the item this digest's reading list has been calling "Bächler 1999 (ENCOP)" conflates a 1999 single-author monograph with a 1990s Swiss research project whose final report was published in 1996 by a different publisher. Anyone citing "the ENCOP report" with a 1999 date is citing neither; the full citation is now in the reading position for next week.

**On length and selection.** Seven developments, five moves, six jurisdictions. Three items — the global El Niño report, the Horn of Africa classification and the Thai floods — come from institutions that produce the field's inputs rather than its arguments, which is the week's own finding about where the field's centre of gravity has moved. One jurisdiction, the United States, produced nothing at all, and a federal shutdown was checked for and ruled out, so the absence is real rather than mechanical.

pushback.target: The reading this digest carried into last week: that the challenge to the climate panel's standing is a challenge from rival scientific bodies, and that the question to ask is who certifies.
pushback.text:
That was wrong, and it was wrong in the way framings usually are — by being a good argument about something that is not happening.

The framing came from a Fijian negotiator's objection, which deserves its own hearing: some countries want scientific bodies other than the panel to guide climate decisions, and small states cannot participate in bodies they have no national equivalent of, so a change of reference body would exclude them from the decisions it informs. That is a real argument and the sentence that carried it — that the Pacific does not have a national space agency — is the best thing a small-state negotiator has said in this digest's run. The error was in treating it as a description of the live mechanism.

Nobody is proposing a substitute body. No state, in any forum this week, tabled an alternative certifier. What is actually being fought over is a date. Five consecutive plenaries have failed to decide whether the next assessment's working-group reports arrive before the second global stocktake closes in 2028 or in 2029, and four proposals are still on the table. The stocktake's political phase ends in 2028, so a 2029 report cannot be an input to it by construction. Nothing is substituted and nothing is dethroned. The panel simply stops being able to speak inside the process that was built to use it, for one cycle.

That matters more than a substitution would, and the difference is worth being precise about. A rival body would be contestable: it would have a name, a membership, a method, and states could refuse to recognise it. A two-year gap is not contestable by anyone. It freezes the evidentiary base that a world court's best-available-science standard, a consensus declaration on sea-level rise, and a loss and damage fund with no other reference all run on. Every entitlement built on assessed science keeps citing a 2021-to-2023 assessment while the climate it describes moves on.

And the second half of the correction is harder, because it cuts against the constituency whose argument this digest was repeating. The states reported to be pressing for the later timetable are China, India, Kenya, Russia and Saudi Arabia, and their stated ground is that developing countries need more time to research, review and approve. That is the capacity argument — the same argument, in the same register, that the small-state objection makes. One constituency invokes capacity to keep the panel central; another invokes capacity to slow it down. Taking capacity as self-evidently the small states' argument was the mistake, and it is the kind of mistake that comes from adopting an actor's framing because the actor is sympathetic.

So: ask about the calendar, not the certifier. And when a negotiator supplies a formulation good enough to quote, check what it is a formulation of.

citation.author: Barry Buzan, Ole Wæver and Jaap de Wilde
citation.title: Security: A New Framework for Analysis
citation.locator: viii, 239 pp.; the environmental sector is chapter 4, opening at p. 71
citation.verification_note: Authors, title, publisher and place confirmed against library catalogue records, which list editions in both 1997 and 1998 under ISBNs 1-55587-603-X and 1-55587-784-2 and give the collation as viii, 239 pages; the field cites 1998 and that is the year carried here. The published contents place the environmental sector as chapter 4, from page 71. The chapter itself could not be opened — the book is in copyright and no reachable library copy would serve it — so the summary below rests on the published contents, on the book's reception, and on David Skidmore's 1999 review in the American Political Science Review. Nothing is quoted as the authors' own wording, and anyone restating the terminology should check it against the original first. The reading list previously gave no publisher and no collation; both have been added, and the closing page range of the environmental chapter is still not asserted.

foundational.summary: This is the Copenhagen School's statement of itself, and the reason it belongs in this sequence rather than in a theory course is that it closes the argument phase 1 left open. Ullman, Mathews, Deudney and Levy argued about whether the environment **is** a security issue. This book declines that question and asks instead how anything becomes one. Security, on its account, is not a condition that obtains but a move an actor makes: naming a referent object as existentially threatened, and thereby claiming the right to measures outside normal politics. Whether the move succeeds depends on an audience accepting it, not on the facts of the threat. The framework then disaggregates security into five sectors — military, political, economic, societal and environmental — each with its own referent objects and characteristic actors, so that "environmental security" stops being one argument and becomes a family of them. The environmental sector gets its own chapter and is generally read as the hardest case in the book: it carries a scientific agenda and a political agenda that are not in register with each other, its referent objects run from a species to a civilisation, and the extraordinary measures the theory predicts mostly fail to arrive. Why it matters here: it supplies the only vocabulary the field has for distinguishing a successful security claim from a loud one, and it treats de-securitisation as a live option rather than a defeat — which is the question every entry in this digest's section C is implicitly asking.
critiques: The speech-act account privileges the moment of utterance and the actors who get to make it, which in practice means state elites with access to a podium. It is poorly equipped to see security being done through bureaucracy, procurement, risk management and insurance rather than through declaration — which is most of what this digest actually records.

The audience is the theory's load-bearing and least specified element. It decides whether a securitising move succeeds, and the framework offers no procedure for identifying it. The European arguments tracked here are addressed to several audiences at once — a parliament, a defence establishment, an insurance market — and the framework cannot say which one's acceptance counts.

Applied to climate, the framework predicts chronic incomplete securitisation, and the field's last two decades have half borne that out. The other half is a problem for it: a binding alliance requirement that carries extreme weather and natural disasters while never using the words "climate change" is not a failed speech act. It is a different mechanism, and a more durable one.

The normative question the framework brackets — whose security, and whether securitising a problem improves anyone's — is the main line of attack from the critical strand that closes this sequence at phase 6, and the framework's own agnosticism about outcomes does not answer it.

foundational.phase: Outside the sequence; nearest to phase 4

foundational.summary: Chosen deliberately against the curriculum item above. Buzan, Wæver and de Wilde ask how something becomes a security issue; this introduces a journal issue whose object is a security institution that has already decided climate is one and is now working out what that obliges it to do. McDonald sets out the axes along which defence establishments engage climate change: new sites of conflict, new operating requirements, new mission types, emissions reduction, and the unglamorous end — estates, infrastructure, procurement, training. He argues the politics of climate security is crucial to how any of it is resolved, and closes by saying defence sectors worldwide will inevitably attend to climate change more. The issue is the first this digest has found to take the defence sector's own climate work as its subject rather than the climate-conflict link, and it is not confined to the Atlantic: one of its articles, by Narayanan, Jayaram and Bharadwaj at 47(1), 108-138, is on militaries in the Bay of Bengal and on climatisation through humanitarian assistance and disaster relief. Read it as the map of a literature that is forming while the institutions it studies are still deciding what to call what they are doing.
critiques: An introduction to a special issue is a map, not a finding. Its claims about the state of the field are editorial, and the evidence sits in articles that were not read here.

"Inevitably" is the weakest word in it. The pattern this digest has accumulated since August is that defence institutions keep the hazard and drop the referent: attention of a kind that does not accumulate into anything citable, and that an annual assessment series used to produce before it quietly stopped.

Spanning the subject from new conflict sites to procurement and training risks collapsing two different objects — what climate does to militaries, and what militaries do about climate. The distinction is the whole policy question, because the first is being funded and the second is being renamed.

developments.title: A famine early-warning system puts the strongest El Niño yet measured on the record, and says the damage arrives later
developments.body: On 6 October the Famine Early Warning Systems Network published a global special report on the food security impacts of the 2026–27 El Niño, which reached very strong levels in September. It puts unimodal East Africa — Ethiopia, South Sudan, Sudan and Karamoja in Uganda — and Southern Africa — Angola, Lesotho, Madagascar, Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia and Zimbabwe — at highest concern; bimodal East Africa including Kenya and Somalia at moderate to high; and West Africa, parts of Latin America and the Caribbean, and Pakistan at moderate. The same day the UN children's agency, the World Food Programme and the Asia-Pacific regional commission put more than 347 million children in nearly a hundred countries and territories inside areas forecast for unusually wet or dry conditions between October and December, about 190 million of them in Asia and the Pacific.
developments.arc_note: The named trend is the one this digest opened a fortnight ago: the institutions that produce the field's inputs — forecasts, observing systems, classification scales — are now making the security argument before any security institution does. This is its clearest instance yet. No ministry, alliance body or council said anything about the strongest El Niño on record this week. A famine early-warning system and three UN agencies did, with named regions and dates attached. The acceleration is in precision, not volume: the warning now specifies which lean season, in which countries, through which crop calendar.

attribution.note: El Niño is a mode of internal climate variability, not an event that can be attributed, and nothing in this week's material claims otherwise: the report attributes the rainfall anomalies to the mode and to its historical analogues, and no event attribution study is claimed or absent. Two cautions follow. The method is analogue years, which assumes historical teleconnections still hold in a warmer atmosphere — a methodological assumption, stated as such in the report's own figure captions, not a hidden one. And the informal label in circulation, "Super El Niño", is doing attribution-shaped work it cannot support: it converts a mode of variability into an emergency without any claim about why the mode is behaving as it is.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The report's own finding on global supply is the opposite of the alarm around it: across strong and very strong El Niño years, global maize, wheat and rice output has changed little on balance, and the US Department of Agriculture projects 2026/27 output 2.7 per cent below last year but still the second largest on record. The hazard in this event is distributional and local, not a global shortfall — which is exactly the distinction Homer-Dixon made in 1994 and the field has spent thirty years re-learning.

source.title: 2026-2027 El Niño food security impacts, Global Special Report

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The operational core of the report is a lag, not a hazard: the most severe food insecurity outcomes from El Niño rainfall anomalies typically emerge during the following lean season rather than during the rainy season itself. That sentence is the entire case for anticipatory action, and it is also the reason anticipatory action keeps failing — the lag that gives governments time to act is the same lag that lets them wait.

source.title: 2026-2027 El Niño food security impacts, Global Special Report

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The children's figures are exposure counts, not impact forecasts, and the agencies say so: more than 347 million children in areas forecast for anomalous conditions October to December, against 1.1 billion already facing at least three overlapping climate hazards. The agencies also put the return on preparedness at up to fifteen dollars saved per dollar spent while less than one per cent of humanitarian funding goes to anticipatory action — a ratio asserted by the appealing parties and not independently sourced in the story.

source.title: From drought to deluge: 'Super' El Niño's expanding reach

claims.label: framing
claims.text: "Super El Niño" is not an official designation and the UN's own story flags it as a label used by some climate watchers. It is nonetheless the term under which the money is being requested, and the agencies publishing the exposure counts are the agencies appealing against them. Neither of those facts makes the counts wrong; both of them mean the label is positioning and should be read as such.

source.title: From drought to deluge: 'Super' El Niño's expanding reach

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No consolidated figure exists anywhere for how much anticipatory money has actually disbursed against this event, as against pledged. The appeal totals, the agency statements and the emergency-fund reporting all count commitments; nothing found counts transfers. For a doctrine whose whole claim is that money moves before the impact, the absence of a disbursement number is the thing that should be embarrassing, and it has been absent all three weeks this digest has looked for it.

nl_eu.note: No Dutch or European link, and the item matters more without one. It sets the clearest test the field will get this year of whether forecast-based financing works when every technical precondition is met at once, and European instruments due this month — a resilience framework built on risk owners and an insurance alliance — are about to make the same bet with the same calendar problem.

developments.title: The Horn's famine risk changes driver from drought to flood without changing magnitude
developments.place: Somalia, with the risk concentrated in the Jubba and Shabelle basins
developments.body: The standing judgement for Somalia going into the Deyr rains is a credible risk of Famine — Phase 5 on the five-point food-security scale — from October 2026 through January 2027, with Emergency the most likely outcome and households already in Catastrophe in Bay, Bakool and the sorghum high-potential agropastoral zones. What has changed is the mechanism. Famine would now become likely through extreme and widespread flooding during the October-to-December rains, destroying crops and cutting communities off from markets and aid, rather than through another failed season. FAO's water and land information unit puts the probability of seasonal rainfall above 300 mm at more than 90 per cent in parts of the south and centre, with an earlier-than-average onset, and names the Jubba and Shabelle catchments. The 2026 main and off-season gu harvest came in about 18 per cent above 2025 and prices are still above historical averages, because the carryover stocks that would absorb a shock are gone.
developments.arc_note: This accelerates a trend this digest named a month ago in a different mountain range: a hazard migrating from the mode a monitoring system was built for to a mode it was not. Somalia's early-warning, classification and financing apparatus was rebuilt after 2011 and again after 2017 around rainfall failure. The thing now forecast to produce famine is rainfall success — too much of it, in named basins, on an early onset. The scenario is in the published outlook, so the apparatus has seen it; what has not been established is whether the trigger protocols that release money are written for it.

attribution.note: No attribution claim is made by anyone and none could be: the event has not happened. The hazard is attributed to the El Niño mode and to analogue years, 1997 and 2023, both of which produced severe Deyr flooding. Worth stating plainly because the asymmetry recurs: the field will have a high-confidence forecast of this event for three months and, if it happens, no event-level attribution of it for a year or more — which is the wrong way round for any instrument that pays on evidence of cause.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: Famine is not the most likely outcome and the early-warning network says so explicitly: Emergency is, with Catastrophe-phase households inside it, and Famine becomes likely only under extreme and widespread Deyr flooding. The scenario structure matters more than the headline, because a conditional projection is what anticipatory financing is supposed to act on and a classification is what it usually waits for.

source.title: Risk of Famine (IPC Phase 5) persists in southern Somalia ahead of October deyr rains, Key Message Update

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: FAO's lead meteorologist on the Somalia unit, Bethwell Mutai, put the forecast's status correctly rather than usefully for fundraising: the resemblance to 1997 and 2023 does not mean flooding is certain, but it says the lead time available must be used to act before impacts occur. An institution that distinguishes a probability from a prediction while asking for money on it is a reliable one, and the distinction is the same one this digest credited to the Himalayan mountain centre in September.

source.title: Strong El Niño weather condition raises risk of severe Deyr flooding in Somalia, FAO warns

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: A better harvest and a worse outlook in the same assessment: gu production about 18 per cent above last year, prices still above historical averages because of low carryover after consecutive poor seasons. This is the clearest available refutation of reading food crisis off production figures, and it is the reason a 2.7 per cent global cereal dip in B1 says almost nothing about whether anyone starves.

source.title: Risk of Famine (IPC Phase 5) persists in southern Somalia ahead of October deyr rains, Key Message Update

claims.label: gap
claims.text: The collective flood anticipatory-action framework and its trigger protocols are reported as still unfinalised, and no trigger document could be found from any agency or from the Somali disaster management agency. What exists is a national El Niño preparedness plan approved in September linking federal, state and local authorities, and no district-level plans with named responsibilities, budgets and timelines. A framework without triggers is a statement of intent; the trigger is the instrument.

claims.label: framing
claims.text: The sharpest formulation of the week came from an environmental expert writing in a Somali outlet on 9 October rather than from any institution: warnings reach capitals faster than they reach villages, and the gap now is delivery. It is advocacy, and it is also the second week running that the last mile has been the binding constraint — in Nepal a warning reached close to a million telephones and was followed by deaths, almost all in landslides. The two cases are a fortnight and a continent apart and the failure is the same shape.

nl_eu.note: European money is in this exposure — British funds for Deyr flood preparedness announced in September, and European contributions through the central emergency response fund — but no European institution has a stake in the trigger question, which is where the outcome will actually be decided. The relevance is precedent: the Union is about to build its own anticipatory architecture on risk owners and insurance, and this is the live test of whether anticipation survives contact with a disbursement calendar.

locations.note: A country mark, deliberately. Nothing had happened anywhere in Somalia by 11 October: this is a forecast and a classification, and the risk is concentrated in the Jubba and Shabelle catchments rather than at the centroid. A point pin here would assert a flood that has not occurred.

developments.dropped: A claim circulating in the same opinion piece that the early-warning network has already shifted the main driver of acute food insecurity from drought to flooding is not what the network's own September update says; the update makes flooding the route to Famine under one scenario, not the current driver. The weaker and sourced version is used. Also dropped: a figure of about 26,000 displaced people in Baidoa facing catastrophic hunger October to December, which appears only in a small outlet attributed to UN humanitarian reporting and could not be confirmed against that reporting.

developments.title: The last talks before Antalya close on an ocean agenda, a pledging round and no reference-science language
developments.place: Nadi, Fiji, with a leaders' segment in Tuvalu
developments.body: The final preparatory meeting before November's climate conference ran 5 to 8 October at Nadi, co-hosted by Fiji, Tuvalu and Australia and funded by Australia, with more than 3,000 delegates against about 300 when Fiji last hosted a pre-conference nine years ago. The agenda that emerged is ocean, overshoot of 1.5°C and access to finance; the meeting endorsed a Taku Pakasoa Declaration calling for deep, rapid and sustained emissions reductions, and the Pacific Islands Forum's own climate fund took new pledges — Fiji US$10 million from its prime minister Sitiveni Rabuka, the United Kingdom £10 million announced by its climate special representative Rachael Kyte, Denmark US$2.3 million, the Netherlands US$1 million, and Ireland doubling an earlier €3 million — reaching about US$190 million against an initial capitalisation target of US$500 million and a long-run US$1.5 billion. Australia's climate minister Chris Bowen, who presides over negotiations at the conference, and Türkiye's environment minister Murat Kurum, its president-designate, visited Tuvalu on 6 October with the heads of the Asian Development Bank and the Green Climate Fund.
developments.arc_note: The named trend is the small-island position's shift away from defending 1.5°C as a threshold with legal character — the form this digest recorded in early September — and towards finance access and the ocean. This week completes that shift. The language that closed the talks is about limiting overshoot and about the ocean's place in the regime, not about the threshold's status, and the concrete output is a pledging round into a regional fund rather than a text about the global goal. Read that as an actor retreating to the asks it can still win, which is a rational move and a loss of the leverage the threshold gave it.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The fund's arithmetic is the item's hardest fact: about US$190 million pledged against a US$500 million initial target and US$1.5 billion long term, after a week in which five donors and the host announced new money. At that rate the first target is a year away and the second is a decade away, and the fund is the Pacific's own instrument rather than one it has to petition.

source.title: New pledges boost Pacific Resilience Facility

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: Australia's president of negotiations gave the week its most compact formulation of the distributional problem: the countries that need the finance most get it least. He said it at the meeting he will chair in November, which makes it a statement of a presidency's own diagnosis rather than an advocacy line.

source.title: Climate needs same urgency as defense spending, COP31 chief says

claims.label: framing
claims.text: Fiji's environment minister closed by saying the meeting showed where progress was possible and where more political courage was needed, that a pre-conference cannot deliver the decisions the Pacific is seeking, and that the region wants the ocean given its rightful place. That is positioning, and it is also an unusually candid admission of what a preparatory meeting is for: the Pacific held a conference in its own region and came away with pledges rather than text.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No outcome text, chair's summary or ministerial statement could be found naming the climate panel as the reference science for climate decisions — which was the first of the four pillars Fiji's chief negotiator set out on 29 September, and the one this digest judged most consequential. What the talks produced instead is a declaration on emissions reductions and a pledging round. The pillar was not defeated; it was not transacted.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: India's environment minister Bhupender Yadav closed with the standard developing-country conditional — India stands ready to work with all parties, and higher ambition must be matched by climate finance, technology transfer and capacity building. Noted here because it is the week's only observable of Indian climate statecraft, and because the same delegation is reported on the slower side of the assessment-timetable argument in B4: ambition conditioned on finance in one forum, review capacity invoked in the other.

Five European states put new money into the Pacific fund during the week, the Netherlands among them at US$1 million. In the same week a draft of the Union's own negotiating position for the conference was reported to say there is no scope for new climate finance commitments (D3). Bilateral generosity into a regional fund and a collective refusal at the multilateral table are both European positions, and the second one is the one that binds.

developments.title: The fight over the reference science is about the calendar, not the certifier
developments.place: Geneva; plenary convening at Addis Ababa
developments.body: On 9 October the climate panel's secretariat issued a media advisory for its sixty-fifth plenary session, at Addis Ababa from 12 to 16 October, with the timetable for its seventh assessment still undecided after five consecutive sessions — Istanbul, Sofia, Hangzhou, Lima and Bangkok. Four proposals remain, according to the panel's chair Jim Skea: two that would deliver all three working-group reports before the second global stocktake concludes in 2028, two that would deliver the impacts and mitigation reports in 2029. A group reported to include China, India, Kenya, Russia and Saudi Arabia argues for the later schedule on the ground that developing countries need more time to research, review and approve; a majority reported to span least-developed countries, small-island states, Vanuatu, the Netherlands and France wants alignment with the stocktake. The synthesis report is unaffected either way and is due by late 2029. The panel's trust fund is separately reported to face a shortfall that could force cuts.
developments.arc_note: Recorded as a correction to this publication rather than as a new development, because the development is that nothing happened for a sixth time and the correction is what the week is actually worth. This digest opened a thread last week on whether the panel remains the reference science, framed around states wanting other scientific bodies to guide decisions. That is not the mechanism under pressure. Nobody is proposing a substitute body in any forum this week. What is being decided is whether the next assessment lands inside the process that uses it. The pushback sets out why the first framing was wrong and what follows from the second.

claims.label: contested
claims.text: This is a real dispute among the people who would have to do the work, and both sides have published grounds. Bill Hare of Climate Analytics argues a majority of countries across geographies and development levels wants alignment and that misalignment with the stocktake would be a major historical break, since the previous assessment was a critical element of the first stocktake. Saudi Arabia has called compressing the cycle improper and Russia has said stocktake inputs are not the key to the panel's success, both per the Earth Negotiations Bulletin's reporting of the plenaries; the stated ground on that side is review and approval capacity in developing countries. Matti Goldberg of the Woodwell Climate Research Center adds a third position that cuts against the majority: even 2028 reports would arrive late in the process. The dispute is over whether assessment quality or assessment timing is the binding constraint on the ambition mechanism, and it has now survived five plenaries unresolved.

source.title: Q&A: Why the standoff between nations over the next IPCC reports matters

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The chair's own account of the previous session is the clearest statement of what kind of failure this is: a frustrating and disappointing meeting, only a business meeting with no science involved in it, whose decisions were more to postpone the decision making than to take decisions, and at which he heard no new arguments. He also named the real obstacle as trust between country groups rather than the technicalities of how a timeline is constructed.

source.title: IPCC: 'Frustrating and disappointing' meeting leaves AR7 timeline in deadlock

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: Two structural facts constrain whatever is decided. The second global stocktake's information phase opens at the November conference, its technical assessment runs from June 2027 to June 2028, and its political phase closes at the 2028 conference — so a 2029 working-group report cannot be an input to it by construction. And the panel's own trust fund is reported heading for depletion before the end of this assessment cycle, which means the body being asked to go faster is also the one being asked to do it on less.

source.title: Q&A: Why the standoff between nations over the next IPCC reports matters

claims.label: framing
claims.text: The small-state objection this digest carried last week — that some countries want scientific bodies other than the panel to guide decisions, and that small states cannot participate in bodies they have no national equivalent of — is a good argument about a different thing. It is positioning against a substitution nobody is currently attempting, and it does not reach the timetable fight, where the capacity argument is being made by the other side and in the name of the same constituency.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: Nothing from any security institution, in any jurisdiction, on what a 2029 assessment would do to the evidentiary base that security-adjacent entitlements now rest on. The 2025 world-court opinion treated the panel's reports as the best available science; the sea-level declaration adopted by consensus in September rests on assessed projections; the loss and damage fund's evidentiary practice has no other reference. A two-year gap in the assessment cycle is a two-year freeze on the science those instruments cite, and no ministry, alliance body or council has said anything about it.

nl_eu.note: The Netherlands and France are reported among the states pressing for completion before the 2028 stocktake, which is the first Dutch position on climate-science governance this digest has been able to record, and it is taken in a scientific-governance forum rather than a security one. For the Union the stake is procedural and large: the resilience framework due this month is to be built on a common 3°C reference trajectory derived from assessed science, so the date of the next assessment sets when that trajectory can next be revised.

developments.title: A foreign minister says climate impacts are being used as a weapon, and seats solar geoengineering at a government climate-security table
developments.body: Opening the eighth Berlin climate and security conference at the German Federal Foreign Office on 6 October, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul argued that actors are using the impacts of climate change as a weapon, and called it a perfidious use of those impacts. He built the case from supply chains rather than from conflict data: drought in Sudan and falling Nile levels, reduced Panama Canal transits cutting daily traffic and vessel draft, El Niño threatening rice, palm oil, coffee and maize harvests in Asia, and the effects of the Strait of Hormuz situation on fertiliser supply and energy prices — Sudan and the Panama Canal, he noted, being some 12,000 km apart. He said investments in climate mitigation are investments in security, and that decentralised renewable generation could become vital to survival if Russia targets Ukraine's energy infrastructure again this winter. He put the Group of Friends on Climate and Security at 81 members, co-chaired with Nauru. And he said solar geoengineering was on the conference's agenda for the first time, covering climate effects, security risks and governance.
developments.arc_note: Novel on both halves. The weaponisation claim is a genuine departure from the field's own vocabulary: threat multiplier names a condition and assigns no agency, while using climate impacts as a weapon names an adversary who is doing something. This digest has recorded two months of climate arguments borrowing other security registers; this is the first time the argument has acquired a perpetrator. And a government-hosted climate-security conference has not previously put solar radiation modification on its programme — the same subject the American climate-security institute is working privately and without minutes on 14 October. Two institutions on two continents reaching the same topic in the same fortnight is where the frame is travelling next.

attribution.note: No attribution study supports the causal chain as stated, and none is claimed. Each link is separately plausible and at least one is well evidenced — Panama Canal transit restrictions under low Gatun water levels have a documented history — but the chain from a warming climate through a specific canal restriction to a specific fertiliser price is not an attributed finding, and the Strait of Hormuz link is not a climate link at all. Recorded as an unattributed causal narrative delivered by a foreign ministry, which is how it will be cited.

claims.label: framing
claims.text: "Using the impacts of climate change as a weapon" is a securitising move of exactly the form section A's framework was written to describe: a referent object named as existentially threatened, an adversary supplied, and a claim on extraordinary measures implied. It is also the register in which a German foreign ministry can speak to a coalition that does not lead with climate, which is the function it is performing. No actor is named as doing the weaponising in the published text, which is what makes it framing rather than evidence.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The Group of Friends on Climate and Security at 81 members is the week's only countable institutional indicator in this field, and the only one in either direction. A group of friends is a low-cost commitment — it binds nobody and spends nothing — so the number measures the breadth of declared interest and not the depth of anything. It is still a number, which is more than the field usually gets.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The instruments the ministry put its name to are all existing ones and all small: the joint UN climate security programme Germany helped establish, which has received $18.27 million in nine years; the Nairobi Toolkit with Kenya inside the Global Counterterrorism Forum; the Weathering Risk peacebuilding initiative; the central emergency response fund's climate action account; and cross-border adaptation and peacebuilding work in Ethiopia, Kenya and Somalia. No new money and no new machinery was announced in the speech.

That is the first instance this digest has recorded of climate adaptation entering a post-conflict reconstruction agenda at ministerial level, and it is the kind of item that produces durable institutional practice precisely because it is unglamorous.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: Nothing was found from any defence ministry, including the German one, engaging the weaponisation claim or the geoengineering session. A foreign ministry arguing to a security audience that climate effects are being weaponised, with no corresponding statement from the ministry that would have to respond, is the familiar shape: the argument is made in the lane where it costs nothing.

nl_eu.note: This is the European Union's largest member state making the field's own argument in the field's own forum, three weeks after the Union's security principal did the same at the General Assembly and a week before a European Council whose agenda carries defence without climate. The pattern is now consistent enough to state: in Europe the climate-security argument is made by foreign ministries and external-action principals, and it does not reach the budget or the defence agenda.

developments.title: Six weeks on, the loss and damage fund has not decided on Nepal, and may not before November
developments.place: Kathmandu; the event in Rasuwa, Nepal
developments.body: As of 8 October the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage had made no decision on Nepal's emergency request, and the board may not decide before or during the November climate conference. The sequence is now dated end to end: the finance and environment ministers wrote to the co-chairs on 31 August asking for a rapid response; board members from the African, Asia-Pacific and least-developed-country constituencies requested an extraordinary meeting on 2 September; the co-chairs replied on 9 September that any options must stay inside existing mandates and procedures; developed-country board members supported convening an urgent consultation on 14 September; nothing since. A separate US$20 million had already been approved under the fund's Barbados Implementation Modalities on earlier Nepali proposals, which is not the emergency request. In the same window Nepal's agriculture and environment ministry put a draft national climate change policy out for comment on 22 September with a ten-day window — six pillars, fifteen themes, 55 strategies, 288 working policies — and on 8 October a former chief of the ministry's climate change management division argued it duplicates existing sector policy and weakens adaptation priority.
developments.arc_note: The repeated pattern is an instrument's calendar against a disaster's. The fund deferred its first funding decision to December, a year after its call opened. Nepal is asking for a decision outside that calendar, which the board has never granted. Nothing about this is a Nepali failure or a board failure in the ordinary sense: the instrument was built to disburse against prepared proposals on an annual cycle and it is being asked to behave like an emergency facility. That mismatch is the same one B1 and B2 describe from the forecasting side, and it is this digest's clearest standing finding.

attribution.note: The attribution network published on 17 September on the Himalayan hazard environment — roughly +1.5°C on July-August temperatures, about +2°C annually, the freezing isotherm rising about 100 m per decade, and the event exceeding the limits of existing risk reduction and early warning — while explicitly declining the event-level counterfactual for the specific rock-ice cascade. That is hazard-environment attribution, not event attribution, and the fund has published no standard for either. Three weeks on, no board, bank or court has reasoned from it.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The dated sequence of letters, requests and replies comes from a former joint-secretary and chief of the climate change management division at Nepal's environment ministry, writing on 8 October, who also led the country's national adaptation plan process. A participant's account rather than a board record, and the most specific public reconstruction available; the fund's own site has still not opened for this routine.

source.title: Making the Climate Change Policy Realistic and Forward Looking

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The human arithmetic has stabilised and it is the identification figure that should be read, not the death toll: 1,453 bodies recovered and more than 5,200 people still unaccounted for a month after the 26 August event, of whom about 112 had been positively identified. A recovery operation that can retrieve fourteen hundred bodies and name a hundred of them is a specific institutional limit, and it bears directly on the evidentiary basis of any compensation claim.

claims.label: framing
claims.text: The draft policy's shape is the familiar response of a state asked to demonstrate readiness to funders: 288 working policies across 55 strategies, produced with consultants engaged by a development bank, out for ten days of comment. The critique from inside the ministry's own lineage — duplication of sector policy, adaptation priority weakened, the 2011 policy not even mentioned — reads the document as an artefact of the financing process rather than of a planning one.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No response from India or China to Nepal's 24 September proposal for a Himalayan climate resilience mechanism, in its third week. Nothing from either capital, and the China-India expert mechanism on trans-border rivers that both governments committed in August to convening in September has still not met. Two refusals of the same thing by the two capitals the proposal names.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The next venue is already fixed and it is a lender's: the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank run in Bangkok from 12 to 18 October, which is where Nepal's published schedule takes its reconstruction argument after the fund's silence. Every institution on that schedule lends, so an argument that succeeds there can still arrive as debt — against the 2015 earthquake precedent of a $250 million grant to a $750 million concessional loan.

nl_eu.note: No direct Dutch or European role, and the precedent is the point. The fund's board is the only standing multilateral body that has to decide what evidence a climate loss requires, and whatever it does with a request backed by hazard-environment attribution and no event-level counterfactual becomes the reference for every later claim — including claims European instruments will have to answer once a resilience framework starts naming risk owners.

developments.title: Bangkok declares a flood disaster and manages it around the arrival of the lenders
developments.place: Thailand, 27 of 77 provinces; Prachinburi and Bangkok worst
developments.body: Thailand's Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation put the death toll from flooding since 16 September at 31 on 5 October and at 60 on 7 October, with rivers still rising in some regions. Flooding was active in 27 of the country's 77 provinces; Prachinburi was worst hit with 19 deaths and more than 188,000 people affected across seven flooded districts, and Bangkok recorded four deaths and declared a city-wide disaster after heavy rain. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul ordered government agencies to manage the flooding and the transport disruption ahead of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, which Bangkok hosts from 12 to 18 October.
developments.arc_note: A repeat pattern, and the repetition is in the governance rather than the water: September is the peak of the Thai rainy season and the country lost more than 160 people to flooding in the south eleven months ago. What makes this instance worth recording is the instruction. A head of government facing sixty deaths in twenty-seven provinces framed the response around the international meeting arriving next week, which is a precise statement of where a flood sits in a middle-income state's order of priorities when both arrive in the same fortnight.

attribution.note: No attribution study exists for this sequence and none is claimed; the reporting makes no climate claim at all and notes only that September is the seasonal peak. Note the cross-signal against B1: the El Niño outlook for Southeast Asia is drought, with rice, palm oil, coffee and maize harvests flagged as at risk, and Thailand is flooding. Both can be true — seasonal anomalies are not uniform across a region — but it is a useful corrective to reading a mode's expected signal as a forecast for any particular country.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The figures are the national disaster agency's own and they doubled inside 48 hours: 31 dead on 5 October, 60 on 7 October, 27 of 77 provinces affected, 19 deaths and over 188,000 people affected in Prachinburi, four deaths and a city-wide disaster declaration in Bangkok.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The prime minister's instruction to agencies named flooding and transport ahead of the monetary fund and bank meetings, which Bangkok hosts 12 to 18 October. The sequencing is the finding, and it is stated in the reporting rather than inferred.

claims.label: framing
claims.text: No climate frame appears anywhere in the Thai coverage of a flood that killed sixty people in three weeks. The absence is worth stating because of what Bangkok is about to host: the two institutions a Himalayan state is taking a loss-and-damage argument to, in a city under a flood declaration, with no participant in either conversation connecting the two. A field that complains about climate securitisation should note how rarely the frame travels when nobody has an interest in moving it.

A figure of more than 4.1 billion baht, about US$122 million, in approved emergency recovery funds appears in secondary reporting and could not be confirmed against a Thai government source.

nl_eu.note: No Dutch or European link. It earns its place by making the week's central argument concrete in a jurisdiction nobody in this field tracks: the gap between a climate hazard and the institutions that could finance a response to it is not only a gap in instruments, it is a gap in attention, and it closes or does not close in the order in which things arrive on a prime minister's desk.

Its output was a paper on 8 October arguing Europe needs a credible alternative when the alliance cannot act, a policy brief on polysilicon supply chains on 6 October, and a podcast on Chinese development cooperation on 5 October co-hosted by the director of its own climate, water and food security programme. Under this digest's standing rule, silence from a research institute between publications is evidence about lead time and not about priorities — but the subject of what it did publish is a priority signal, and it is raw materials and alliance contingency.

If an insurance alliance is stood up on 28 October without specifying an independent basis for loss estimation, the private number becomes the official one by default.

claims.text: "No scope" is a negotiating position and not a budget, and it is being taken in the same month as a defence-weighted European Council and a special budget summit in November. Read charitably it is honesty about fiscal space; read as positioning it forecloses, before the conference opens, the one thing the host presidency and the Pacific have both named as the test. Which reading is right is answerable on 12 October, because a draft is where a position is strongest and adopted conclusions are where it is paid for.

moves.title: The German Federal Foreign Office convenes the eighth Berlin climate and security conference
moves.actor: Federal Foreign Office, Germany, with adelphi; Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul opening
moves.body: Held on 6 October under the theme "A climate for security, freedom and prosperity", in person by invitation and streamed, the eighth edition ran sessions on climate adaptation as a strategic advantage for energy supply and defence, climate-resilient reconstruction in Syria with Syrian representatives present, climate effects feeding extremism and terrorism — a breakout with the UN disarmament research institute and the Global Community Engagement and Resilience Fund — and economic security with an emphasis on food. Solar geoengineering appeared on the programme for the first time. The conference has no standing output document; its results are to feed into the November climate conference and a UN water conference in Abu Dhabi in December. Eleven of the fourteen governments funding the UN's joint climate-security programme are European and the Netherlands is not one of them; Germany is, and helped establish it.
moves.stated_rationale: That national and human security must be considered together, and that investments in climate mitigation and resilience are investments in security — the opening statement's formulation. The programme's own framing is that insights from the April New York edition should be brought into dialogue with defence, civil society, researchers, the private sector and finance actors, and that the results should inform the November conference and the December water conference.
moves.inference: A foreign ministry holding its eighth annual climate-security convening inside a coalition that does not lead with climate is doing two things at once, and only one of them is about climate. The theme's three nouns — security, freedom, prosperity — are a domestic settlement, not an analysis. What the ministry gets from the format is standing in a field it helped build, at the cost of a convening and no new money; what the field gets is a government venue where solar geoengineering can be discussed on the record, which is more than the American institute's unminuted tabletop eight days later will provide. The weaponisation claim in B5 is the ministry's bid to make the argument legible to a defence audience, and the test of whether it lands is whether any defence ministry repeats it. Treat the absence of an output document as deliberate and as the reason eight editions have produced influence nobody can trace.

moves.title: The November conference's president-designate prices the climate finance ask in the alliance's defence commitment
moves.actor: Murat Kurum, Minister of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change of Türkiye and COP31 president-designate
moves.body: Speaking to reporters at the close of the preparatory talks on 8 October, the conference's president-designate said governments should show the same commitment to climate action that they show to defence, and asked: "What does it mean to spend 5% for defense if you don't have a country to live on?" The 5 per cent is the alliance's Hague commitment — at least 3.5 per cent of national output on core defence by 2035 plus 1.5 points on defence- and security-related areas including resilience. His own formulation of the ask was "the same responsibility, same determination, we expect each and every country to show in climate action". The collective finance goal he set it against is $1.3 trillion a year to developing countries by 2035. In the same week a draft of the European Union's negotiating position was reported to say there is no scope for new climate finance commitments at the conference.
moves.stated_rationale: That the urgency governments have found for defence spending is the urgency climate finance requires, and that the existing collective finance goal is the measure against which the conference should be judged. He pairs it with his presidency's two launched pledges, on electrification and on artificial intelligence.
moves.inference: This is the clearest reversal this digest has recorded of the pattern it has been tracking since August. For two months the traffic ran one way: climate arguments reached for energy-supply, economic-security and resilience language because the field's own register was unavailable in the room. Here a climate conference presidency reaches into the defence budget, and specifically into the one number every European and North American treasury has already conceded. It is an argument from precedent rather than from threat: not that climate is a security problem, but that the political capacity to find five per cent of national output exists and has been demonstrated. That is a stronger argument than the threat-multiplier case and it is available to anyone. The risk in it is the one the critical strand has always named: an ask framed against a defence benchmark invites the answer that climate money should come out of the 1.5 points, which is what the alliance's own centre of excellence is convening a summit about on 15 and 16 October, and what the military council argued a year ago before going silent. A presidency that borrows the defence register may find the defence sector has already spent the borrowing. Note also what the move is not: it is rhetoric from a presidency whose own division of labour with Australia is publicly contested, and no money followed it.

moves.title: The Union's draft negotiating position forecloses new climate finance before the conference opens
moves.actor: Council of the European Union, drafting conclusions for the Environment Council of 12 October
moves.body: A draft of the Union's negotiating position for the November conference, reported on 6 October from a copy seen by Bloomberg, says there is no scope for new climate finance commitments at the conference and puts the emphasis on implementing existing decisions and a short list of concrete tasks. The same draft seeks the mitigation work programme, whose mandate ends at this conference, extended to at least 2040, and the second global stocktake set up. Environment ministers were to review preparations in Luxembourg on 12 October, where conclusions on the Union's main negotiating positions for the climate and biodiversity conferences are to be approved alongside the proposed review of the emissions trading system. Separate reporting records German climate spending falling last year and a missed German climate financing pledge.
moves.stated_rationale: Implementation over new pledges: that the task at Antalya is to operationalise what has already been agreed, extend the mitigation work programme and prepare the stocktake, rather than to add commitments. No fiscal rationale is given in what has been reported of the draft.
moves.inference: Read it against D2 and the week has a clean pair. The host presidency's argument is that the political capacity for large commitments has been demonstrated in defence and should be found for climate; the Union's drafters have decided in advance that it will not be. That is not hypocrisy, it is a budget: the Union is simultaneously negotiating a long-term financial framework, a defence build-up and an insurance-based climate resilience framework due on 28 October, and the resilience framework is the tell. An instrument built on named risk owners, member-state resilience plans and an insurance alliance is a design for allocating existing risk rather than for financing new transfers. Foreclosing finance at Antalya while standing up an insurance architecture at home is a coherent strategy and an answer to the question this digest has asked all autumn about which register European climate policy is written in: neither security nor solidarity, but risk management. The thing to watch is whether the phrase survives ministers, because a draft is where a position is strongest and conclusions are where it is actually paid for.

moves.title: Fiji converts its four-pillar position into a pledging round and an ocean agenda
moves.actor: Lynda Tabuya, Fiji's minister for information, environment and climate change and chair of the Pacific small island developing states, with Sivendra Michael, permanent secretary and chief negotiator
moves.place: Nadi, Fiji, with a leaders' segment in Tuvalu
moves.body: The four pillars set out on 29 September were science and 1.5°C, finance, oceans and Pacific leadership. What the talks delivered, across 5 to 8 October, was the second and third: new pledges into the Pacific Islands Forum's own climate fund from Fiji at US$10 million, the United Kingdom at £10 million, Denmark at US$2.3 million, the Netherlands at US$1 million and Ireland doubling an earlier €3 million, taking the fund to about US$190 million against a US$500 million initial target; a Taku Pakasoa Declaration endorsed by thirty jurisdictions calling for deep, rapid and sustained emissions reductions; and work on the ocean-climate nexus and on limiting overshoot. No outcome language on the climate panel as the reference science could be found. Tabuya closed saying the meeting showed where progress was possible and where more political courage was needed, and that a pre-conference cannot deliver the decisions the Pacific seeks.
moves.stated_rationale: Keep 1.5°C within reach, make finance reach the communities that need it, and give the ocean its rightful place in the climate regime — her three opening messages on 5 October, carried through to the close. The underlying position is that the Pacific's leverage lies in hosting and in its own instruments rather than in petitioning.
moves.inference: Landed on the asks that were winnable and abandoned, for now, the one that was not. A regional fund at US$190 million is an instrument the Pacific controls, which is worth more per dollar than a line in a conference text, and the ocean pillar is the one on which Türkiye's presidency has an interest in agreeing. The science pillar — the defence of the climate panel as the reference body — simply did not get transacted, which is consistent with the correction in this week's pushback: it was aimed at a substitution nobody is attempting while the real decision sat in a scientific-governance plenary four days later. The chairmanship arithmetic is worth holding: the Pacific negotiating bloc's chair and the host ministry are the same office, which concentrates the regional position in one person two months before Antalya and makes it fragile to a reshuffle.

moves.title: A fifth straw poll on the succession, and the leader loses ground
moves.actor: The UN Security Council under the Greek presidency; Ambassador Aglaia Balta presiding
moves.body: The Council held its fifth straw poll on candidates for Secretary-General on 7 October, in the consultations room, with seven candidates and none withdrawn since the fourth: Ivonne A-Baki and María Fernanda Espinosa Garcés of Ecuador, Rafael Mariano Grossi of Argentina, Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica, Olara Otunnu of Uganda, Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett of Guyana and Macky Sall of Senegal. Results are not released officially; reporting gives Grynspan at nine encourage, six discourage and none without opinion, down from ten encourage on 29 September; Grossi at six, seven and two, down from eight encourage; and Rodrigues Birkett at five, nine and one, her worst of the five polls. A sixth poll is set for 16 October and Council diplomats say it may be colour-coded, separating the permanent members' ballots from the rest without identifying individual states. The current Secretary-General's term ends on 31 December.
moves.stated_rationale: The Greek presidency named making progress on, or agreeing, the appointment as October's substantive business. Straw polls are the Council's own device for narrowing a field without a formal vote.
moves.inference: The field is not converging, it is eroding: four of the seven lost ground between the fourth poll and the fifth, including both front-runners, which is the signature of a Council testing whether anyone can clear a veto rather than of one choosing. The move towards colour-coded ballots is the tell — it is asked for when members suspect the discouragement sits with a permanent member and want to know before spending more capital. For this field the finding is unchanged and getting more expensive: the institution that houses the only standing multilateral climate-security machinery, funded at $18.27 million over nine years, may have a new head within weeks, and the 2021 veto means Council competence over climate is a live inheritance. Nobody has asked any of the seven about either, in public, through five polls.

roster_silences:
Worked this week, and what the standing roster produced was mostly absence. Two of those absences are findings and the rest are lead time; the distinction is whether the institution had published a schedule.

**Findings.** The International Military Council has now been silent for twelve months — no report since the 2024 edition of its annual flagship, and no item of any kind since an open letter of 23 October 2025 arguing for clean energy investment to count inside the alliance's non-core defence spending. Next week the alliance's own climate change and security centre of excellence convenes a summit on climate-smart defence investment on the road to five per cent, which is that letter's argument with a venue. A body with a named chair, a named secretary general and a standing report series has gone quiet for the year in which its position became somebody else's conference. Separately, the alliance's annual climate and security assessment remains unpublished since 2024 with no statement ever made about it; that series had a schedule, and the schedule was the commitment.

**Lead time, not findings.** The Stockholm institute's climate, peace and security list still ends at the August Abyei study. The attribution network has published nothing since 17 September, including nothing on the Horn of Africa forecast and nothing on Europe's heat season — and the question to ask of an attribution network is not whether it published this week but whether it has declined a case it was asked to take, which it has not. The Himalayan mountain centre published nothing on its own region. The alliance's centre of excellence welcomed its 2026 fellows on 6 October and published nothing. The Hague strategic studies centre published on alliance contingency planning and on polysilicon supply chains and nothing on climate.

**Neither, and worth naming as a third category.** The Dutch institute whose climate-security platform this digest tracks refused retrieval for a fifth consecutive week. That is not silence and not output; it is a hole in the observation, and recording it as a finding about the institute would be a finding about this routine instead. The platform's own separate site opened, as it has before, and carries curated work by other institutions rather than its own.

**And one absence that is about allocation rather than silence.** The American climate-security institute published no research this week — a media round-up and an event recap — while its parent opened a second cohort of a fellowship on artificial intelligence and national security. That is three weeks without a state-level briefer. An institute that publishes nothing has lead time. An institute whose new programme capacity goes somewhere else has made a choice.

**Still unfilled on the roster:** a named contact at the Pacific Islands Forum secretariat itself, as against the Fijian ministers, and the head of the UN's joint climate-security programme — which, given that the programme has received $18.27 million in nine years and was cited again this week by a European foreign minister as evidence of commitment, is the highest-value gap on the list.
