active_trends.text: Removal of climate from security vehicles rather than only from language. No new instance and no reversal on either side of the Atlantic this week. The American defence establishment produced nothing in either direction; the European separation showed up in agenda form instead, with defence and security on the European Council's 15 and 16 October agenda and climate in a separate council three days earlier. Agenda separation is a weaker observable than a deleted referent and is recorded as the weaker thing.

US adaptation surviving only where reframed as disaster operations. No federal observable. At the institute level the reframing has not continued either: a third week with no state-level briefer, and the organisation's new programme capacity went to a fellowship on artificial intelligence and national security. The trend may be ending not because the reframing failed but because the subject has been displaced.

Security Council shift from climate security to natural resource governance, and now past it. Confirmed against the Council monitor's own October forecast: the month's programme carries no climate, water, food-security or environment item in any framing, and the two signature events are on children in armed conflict and on emerging technologies with a maritime emphasis. The resource framing has not replaced the climate framing; both are absent.

Retreat from binding multilateral environmental instruments, and this week it reached the science that binds them. Five consecutive plenaries of the climate panel have failed to set the timetable for the next assessment, with a group including China, India, Kenya, Russia and Saudi Arabia pressing for delivery after the 2028 stocktake rather than before it. Nobody is proposing to leave an instrument; the effect of a two-year gap in assessed science is to loosen every instrument that cites it without any state having to withdraw from anything.

Dutch institutional creation with fiscal non-commitment. Confirmed again and in a new venue. The €5 million structural defence line stands and its action plan is now three months and one week overdue. Abroad, the Netherlands pledged US$1 million to the Pacific's own climate fund — a real commitment, the smallest of five made that week, and two tenths of one per cent of that fund's initial target. The pattern is not absence of money; it is money at an order of magnitude that cannot change an outcome, attached to a position that can be cited.

Dutch public-opinion decline against the international average. Not refreshed this week; the evidence is now five months old and unchanged since the May survey. Recorded so the age of the evidence stays visible rather than the claim hardening by repetition.

Overshoot moving from a risk to a planning premise. Advanced from an unexpected direction: the Pacific's own preparatory meeting worked on limiting the overshoot of 1.5°C as an agenda item, which is the constituency with the most to lose from conceding the premise doing so in its own forum. The European instrument due 28 October is still reported to carry a 3°C reference trajectory for 2100. Within six weeks the premise has been adopted by the agency that first published it, the bloc that will legislate on it, and the states that refused it.

High-mountain hazard migrating from the mode monitoring was built for to the mode it was not. No new high-mountain instance this week, and the same mismatch appeared in a different hazard class and a different continent: Somalia's famine early-warning and financing apparatus, rebuilt twice around rainfall failure, is now forecasting famine through rainfall excess. The generalised form of this trend is the one to carry: an early-warning system is built around a hazard mechanism, and the mechanism moves.

The gap between what event attribution will certify and what climate finance is asked to pay for. Unchanged and sharpened by a new asymmetry. For the Somali Deyr the field will have a high-confidence seasonal forecast for three months before the event and, if it happens, no event-level attribution for a year after it — forecast confidence and attribution confidence arriving in the wrong order for any instrument that pays on evidence of cause. Three weeks after the Himalayan hazard-environment study, no board, bank or court has reasoned from it.

Climate argued in whichever security register is locally unoccupied rather than in the field's own. This week the traffic reversed and the trend needs restating to cover both directions. The November conference's president-designate priced the climate finance ask against the alliance's 5 per cent defence commitment, and a foreign minister told a security audience that climate impacts are being used as a weapon — a formulation that supplies an adversary where threat multiplier supplies only a condition. So the rule is not that climate borrows other registers; it is that the argument is made in whichever register the audience already concedes. Where that is energy supply, it is energy supply; where a defence budget has just been tripled, it is a defence budget.

The assets a changing hazard environment destroys are increasingly publicly indispensable and privately owned, with no instrument settling who pays. Not advanced this week, and one figure withdrawn: the reconstruction requirement circulating for the Nepali event could not be confirmed against any government document and is not carried. What did advance is adjacent and worse — of about 1,453 bodies recovered, roughly 112 had been identified, which is a limit on the evidentiary basis of any claim at all, private or sovereign.

The climate referent and the security register being decoupled, in both directions, by different actors in the same week. Still running and now with a third mode. A foreign ministry re-coupled them explicitly, naming climate and claiming a weapon; the Union decoupled them administratively, putting defence on one council's agenda and climate on another's. Neither is a deletion. The referent is being routed, not removed, and the routing is visible in agendas before it is visible in texts.

The contest is moving from the hazard to the apparatus that measures and prices it. The strongest week yet, in a new form. The institutions that produced this week's security argument were a famine early-warning network, a food and agriculture meteorological unit and three UN agencies — not a ministry, an alliance or a council. And the apparatus itself is now what states are negotiating over: the climate panel's assessment timetable, five plenaries unresolved, with its trust fund reported heading for depletion. Whoever sets when the science arrives sets what every instrument citing it can say, and that is now a dated, contested, state-level decision.

Forecast quality and institutional calendars have come apart, and the field's central operational doctrine sits in the gap. Anticipatory action assumes that a confident forecast plus lead time produces money before impact. This week supplied the most favourable conditions that assumption will ever get — a very strong El Niño, named basins, specified measures, published scenarios, months of warning — alongside three instruments that cannot move on that clock: a loss and damage board that has never granted an out-of-cycle decision, six weeks into a sovereign emergency request; a collective flood trigger protocol still unfinalised eight weeks from the rains; and no published figure anywhere for how much anticipatory money has actually disbursed rather than been pledged. The trend to watch is not whether forecasts improve. It is whether any disbursement calendar is ever rewritten to match one.

open_threads.text: PSI's current funding phase. Unmoved, and the hole in the observation is now five weeks deep: the institute's own domain refused retrieval again. The platform's separate site opened and carries curated work by other institutions and nothing on its own resourcing. The last publicly datable announcement of a funding phase remains December 2019. Five refusals is not a finding about the institute; it is a statement that one route has failed and the sister-site route answers a different question.

Whether NATO published a fourth Climate Change and Security Impact Assessment. Still no, still no statement, and the displacing question now has a date. The alliance's own climate change and security centre of excellence welcomed its 2026 cohort of fellows on 6 October, published nothing, and convenes its defence-climate summit in Montréal on 15 and 16 October under a title built around climate-smart investment on the road to 5 per cent, with a Nordic resilience and infrastructure workshop the day before. The alliance's climate work plainly continues; the thing that stopped is the one public, citable, annual judgement.

Whether the International Military Council's World Climate and Security Report has formally lapsed. Sixth consecutive week of silence: no report since the 2024 edition and the most recent item of any kind still the open letter of 23 October 2025. Next week the alliance's own centre of excellence convenes the summit on climate-smart defence investment that the letter effectively argued for. A body with a named chair, a named secretary general and a standing report series has now been silent for a year while its position became someone else's conference.
Funding trajectory of the joint United Nations climate security unit.
open_threads.resolution: Answered in magnitude, by a printed portfolio report rather than by the dashboard that has refused to render for three weeks. Cumulative deposits to the joint programme between 2016 and 2024 were $18.27 million, which places it thirteenth of fifteen funds in the trust fund office's climate and environment portfolio, against $808.89 million for the largest and about $2 million a year for this one. Fourteen governments contribute, eleven of them European; the Netherlands is not among them. The programme is not being wound down — a third phase runs 2026 to 2028 with ten advisers deployed — and it is funded at the level of a mid-sized national research grant. One consequence for this digest's own published record: Britain's £1 million of 25 September, reported here as three tenths of one per cent of a £331 million package and treated as a rounding error, is on the order of 5 per cent of everything this programme has ever received. The denominator was wrong. What remains unanswered is the year-by-year trajectory and whether the third phase has a stated requirement, which is carried forward as a separate question.

open_threads.text: Whether the 2028-2034 budget carries a security-tagged climate line. Not advanced internally, and the first dated negative arrived from outside it: a draft of the Union's negotiating position for the November conference is reported to say there is no scope for new climate finance commitments. That is about external finance rather than the internal budget, but the two are drawn from the same fiscal space, and the special European Council on the long-term budget falls on 26 and 27 November. The nearer instrument, the resilience framework of 28 October, is still expected to arrive with an insurance architecture rather than a budget line.

Chinese defence doctrine on climate — gap, eighth week, and the question has now been answered in the negative well enough to retire the instrument. No white paper, no doctrinal text, nothing. The two substitutes are both producing dated observables: the China-India expert mechanism on trans-border rivers, committed in August to meeting in September, is now two months past its own deadline with no meeting found from any ministry on either side; and China is reported among the states pressing for the climate panel's next assessment to land after the 2028 stocktake rather than before it. Chinese climate positions exist. They are taken in water diplomacy and in science governance.

Any Indian security document on climate — gap, eighth week, and one of the two better instruments has now been verified. India's reported resistance to completing the next assessment before the 2028 stocktake, with China, Kenya, Russia and Saudi Arabia, rested last week on a newsletter; it now rests on reporting of the plenaries by a specialist outlet citing the Earth Negotiations Bulletin, which is a step up and still not a plenary record. A third instrument is added and it is the strongest yet: the 1996 Ganges treaty expires in December, India says the matter runs through the joint rivers commission, and Bangladesh says it wants a new treaty rather than a renewal.
Swiss Re sigma citation for the $424bn 2025 protection gap.
open_threads.resolution: The citation is **sigma 1/2026**, *Natural catastrophes in 2025: the persistent rise of wildfire and storm risk*, Swiss Re Institute. The protection gap of $424 billion for 2025, up from $395 billion in 2024, with the natural catastrophe resilience index broadly stable at 27.3 per cent, comes from the Institute's Natural Catastrophe Insurance Resilience Index and is expressed in premium-equivalent terms. Caveat on strength: the reinsurer's own page would not open and the mirrored PDF's text could not be extracted, so the figures are corroborated across Swiss Re's own social post and several independent trade reports rather than read off the document.

open_threads.text: Whether any event attribution study of the 26 August Langtang-Lirung cascade appears.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved on 17 September 2026, and the answer is not one of the two the thread was framed to expect. World Weather Attribution published *Rapid Warming in the Himalaya Exacerbates Geohazard Cascades Beyond Adaptation Limits*, with contributors in ten countries across glaciology, mountain hydrology, climate science, seismology, humanitarian practice and social science. It attributes the hazard environment and not the event: about 1.5°C added to July-August temperatures by human-caused climate change, about 2°C annually — larger than global mean warming — individual winter months as much as 3°C, and the 0°C isotherm rising roughly 100 metres a decade into the bedrock that failed. It states explicitly that it has not assessed whether this specific rock-ice avalanche would have occurred without human-induced climate change, while asserting that warming at a rate beyond the global mean increases the likelihood and severity of such hazards. It then concludes that the event exceeded the design and predictive limits of existing risk reduction, that no existing early warning system could have provided sufficient lead time, that this constitutes a soft limit to adaptation given constrained habitable land and population increase, and that addressing loss and damage through recovery and reconstruction has become an unavoidable part of climate response. So: no event attribution, a hazard-environment attribution, and the policy conclusion reached through adaptation limits instead of causation. The successor question is the `adaptation-limits-adjudication` thread. Reporting figures that travelled with it: the debris flood ran 200 km in under seven hours at average speeds around 188 km/h and deposited 30.5 million cubic metres of material.

open_threads.text: What the HiRISK consortium is: membership, funding, institutional home.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved from hirisk.org, which was opened and read. HiRISK describes itself as 'a loose consortium of experts from High Mountain Asia and beyond', producing open risk datasets, dashboards, an expert database, risk assessments and peer-reviewed papers. Its listed member organisations include the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, the University of Central Asia in Tajikistan, a research group in Pakistan, a mountain-hazards institute in China, a hydrological institute in Bhutan, and two regional agencies including the Aga Khan Agency for Habitat. Stated support comes from Geo Mountains and from the Glacier and Permafrost Hazards in Mountains standing group of the International Association of Cryospheric Sciences and the International Permafrost Association. Funding amounts and sources are not disclosed, no individuals are named, and the site is labelled beta. Cite it as a consortium finding attributed to the consortium; do not upgrade it to institutional authority.

open_threads.text: What standard of evidence the loss and damage fund applies to a claim from an event with no event-level attribution. Unchanged and now the live question rather than a demoted one. Six weeks after Nepal's emergency request the board has not decided and may not before the November conference; three weeks after the Himalayan hazard-environment study, no board, bank or court has reasoned from it. A new dimension appeared this week from the recovery side: of about 1,453 bodies recovered, roughly 112 had been positively identified. Whatever standard the board eventually applies, a claim's evidentiary base is also limited by what a disaster response can establish about who was lost.

Whether any part of the deltacommissaris's ask — 1 per cent of national output to at least 2 — survives into a government commitment. Fourth checkpoint passed in silence: no cabinet response to the 2027 programme, against a one-day turnaround in 2025, and nothing on water in the responsible committee. The autumn budget rounds on infrastructure and water fall later, so some of this is calendar; four checkpoints is past the point where calendar explains it.

Whether an adaptation-limits argument is adjudicable by the institutions that will now receive it. Unchanged. The only route identified remains the European framework of 28 October, whose named risk owners would create an administrative respondent to the question of whether a given loss exceeded feasible adaptation. Nothing this week from any fund board, bank, insurer or court.

Who bears roughly Rs300 billion of privately held losses in Nepal, and whether a sovereign loss and damage claim can cover them. Unmoved on the instrument and one figure withdrawn. A reconstruction requirement of NRs 559.18 billion, about US$3.62 billion, is circulating in commentary and could not be confirmed against any Nepali government document; a separate explainer projects US$4 to 5 billion. Neither is carried here, and the US$4.7 billion this digest used in earlier weeks measured damage rather than reconstruction need. The assessed split — about seventy per cent of about Rs408 billion on the private sector, with 759 MW of damaged generation — stands as the only sourced arithmetic.

Whether any security institution reads the sea-level declaration as a security instrument. The strongest available negative is now confirmed against the Council monitor's own October forecast rather than against a presidency's announcement: the month's programme carries no climate, water, food-security or environment item in any framing, under a maritime state's presidency, three weeks after the declaration was adopted by consensus. Nothing from any other security institution either.

Whether NATO's removal of the climate referent from its resilience baseline is a one-off drafting choice or standing practice. Nothing from the alliance, and the test is now four days away: the centre of excellence's Montréal summit of 15 and 16 October names climate throughout its own framing. If the centre says climate freely while the binding requirements do not, the removal was a drafting discipline applied to instruments that bind rather than a change in what the alliance thinks.
Whether money reaches Somalia before the October-to-December rains.
open_threads.resolution: Answered yes, in part, and the answer required correcting this digest. Money did move before the rains: $7 million was pre-approved from the central emergency response fund in June for flood response preparedness ahead of the El Niño, alongside $10 million for drought response, and on 24 September Britain announced £5 million specifically for Deyr flood preparedness, split equally between a health, nutrition, water and protection programme led by Action Against Hunger and a Shabelle-basin rehabilitation programme delivered through three agencies, expected to reach about 600,000 people. Last week's digest said the money had not come; it had, one day before that was written. The proportions still carry the original finding: about £5 million and $7 million of anticipatory money against 2.5 to 3.5 million people exposed, roughly a million expected to be displaced, and a humanitarian plan at about a quarter funded. What happens next — whether the forecast verifies and whether the anticipatory money measurably reduced loss — is carried forward as a new question rather than as this one.

open_threads.text: Whether India or China responds to Nepal's proposal for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, made from the General Assembly rostrum on 24 September. Third week, nothing from either capital, and the bilateral mechanism the proposal would build on is itself two months past a commitment to meet. One adjacent signal worth noting: Nepali commentary is beginning to reframe the proposal as a risk-intelligence system rather than a mechanism, which is what a proposal does when it is not answered — it becomes a domestic capability argument instead of a diplomatic one.

Whether the joint United Nations climate-security programme's third phase has a stated funding requirement, and whether contributions into it are rising, flat or falling. Unchanged; the route remains identified and not taken. The programme was named again this week, by the German foreign minister, among the instruments his ministry stands behind — which is the eighth consecutive week in which the programme is cited as evidence of commitment by governments that have put $18.27 million into it over nine years, with the Netherlands not among the fourteen contributors.

Whether the climate panel remains the reference science for climate decisions, on what timetable, and which states are pressing on each axis. Substantially reframed this week, and the reframing is a correction to this publication; the pushback sets it out. Nobody is proposing a substitute body in any forum. What is contested is the date: five consecutive plenaries have failed to decide whether the next assessment's working-group reports land before the 2028 stocktake or in 2029, four proposals remain on the table, and the panel's trust fund is reported heading for depletion before the cycle ends. The security stake is unchanged and is about dates rather than identity — the 2025 world-court opinion's best-available-science standard, the sea-level declaration's presumptions and the loss and damage fund's evidentiary practice would all run on a 2021-23 assessment for another cycle.

Whether any security institution treats the meteorological observing system's radio spectrum as an asset to be defended before the 2027 radiocommunication conference. Nothing new, and a partial answer surfaced from an unexpected direction while verifying something else. The July analysis of the Dutch defence climate strategy by the director of the Hague centre's climate, water and food security programme names reliable climate, weather and ocean data as a dependency the strategy barely addresses, and points at cuts to American observing systems. That is a defence-adjacent institution naming the observing system as a vulnerability, three months before the two UN agencies escalated on spectrum. It is an analyst rather than a ministry, and it is the first thing found on this axis at all.

Whether any public institution produces an estimate of what Europe's 2026 heat season cost, to set against the private one. Unchanged, and the deadline is now a fortnight away. The only figure in circulation is an insurer's — about €113 billion of annual output across thirty countries, from proprietary damage functions — and the statistical office, the environment agency and the national meteorological services have still converted nothing. If the framework of 28 October stands up a climate insurance alliance without specifying an independent basis for loss estimation, the private number becomes the official one by default.

Whether the Somali Deyr forecast verifies and whether the anticipatory money measurably reduced loss. Advanced, and the question is now sharper than when it was opened. The classification has changed mechanism: famine would become likely through extreme and widespread flooding rather than through another failed season, with Emergency the most likely outcome and Catastrophe-phase households already in Bay, Bakool and the sorghum agropastoral zones. Against that, the collective flood anticipatory-action framework and its trigger protocols are reported still unfinalised eight weeks from the peak, and no district-level plans with named responsibilities, budgets and timelines could be found. The test is no longer only whether the money worked; it is whether a trigger exists to release it.

Whether any candidate for Secretary-General states a position on climate, and in particular on Security Council competence over it. Fifth straw poll on 7 October, seven candidates, none withdrawn, the leader down from ten encourage to nine and four of seven losing ground; a sixth poll on 16 October, possibly colour-coded. Nothing found on any candidate's climate position, from the Council, the Assembly or their own material. Five polls, eleven weeks to the end of the incumbent's term, and the question unasked in public.

Whether the climate panel's plenary at Addis Ababa, 12 to 16 October, decides the timetable for its next assessment, and on which side. Four proposals are on the table: two deliver all three working-group reports before the second global stocktake closes in 2028, two deliver the impacts and mitigation reports in 2029. The stocktake's information phase opens at the November conference and its political phase closes in 2028, so a 2029 report cannot inform it by construction. Two subsidiary questions with the same answer date: whether the review of the panel's own principles and procedures is taken up or deferred for a third time, and whether anything is said about the trust fund reported heading for depletion. A decision was wanted by the end of 2026 and this is the last scheduled plenary before the conference.

Whether the Union's reported position that there is no scope for new climate finance commitments at the November conference survives into adopted conclusions, and whether it holds at Antalya. The draft was reported on 6 October from a copy seen by a financial wire; environment ministers were to approve conclusions on 12 October. Two things to read in whatever is adopted: whether the phrase is still there, and whether the mitigation work programme extension to at least 2040 is traded for it. The wider question is what it means that the bloc which supplies most of this field's vocabulary and personnel arrived at the conference having pre-emptively ruled out the thing both the host presidency and the Pacific have named as the test.

Whether the 1996 Ganges treaty is renewed, replaced or allowed to lapse, and on what terms. It expires in December 2026 — sources give 12 December and 31 December and do not agree, which is itself worth settling. India says the matter runs through the joint rivers commission; Bangladesh's water resources minister says Dhaka wants a new treaty with guarantee clauses on dry-season flows rather than a renewal; West Bengal has objected to the centre proceeding without the state, having blocked a comparable arrangement before. The dry-season sharing formula, the treaty's duration and any move towards basin-wide governance are the live disagreements. This is the largest dated transboundary water decision in the field's calendar and the first in this digest's run that falls due inside a quarter.

Whether anyone publishes how much anticipatory climate money has actually disbursed, as against pledged. Three weeks of looking has produced appeal totals, pledge tallies and emergency-fund allocations, and no figure anywhere for transfers made before an impact. The doctrine's whole claim is that money moves early; the number that would demonstrate it is not kept in public by any agency, fund or donor found so far. Until it is, every statement about forecast-based financing working is a statement about intentions. The Somali Deyr is the best available natural experiment and the figure would have to exist by about February 2027 to be worth anything.

Whether solar radiation modification's arrival in government climate-security forums is a one-off or the start of an agenda. In one fortnight it appeared on the programme of a foreign ministry's annual climate-security conference for the first time, on 6 October, covering climate effects, security risks and governance; and as the subject of a private, unminuted tabletop exercise run by an American climate-security institute with a solar-geoengineering research organisation on 14 October. The two formats differ in exactly the way that matters: one produces a record and one is designed not to. What to watch is whether any state, alliance body or multilateral institution puts a position on paper, and whether the research organisations convening these discussions are ever distinguished from the parties with an interest in the technique's efficacy.

Whether the Pacific Islands Forum's own climate fund reaches its US$500 million initial capitalisation target by the end of 2026, as its board intends, from about US$190 million after this week's pledging round. It matters beyond the Pacific because it is the clearest test available of whether a regional fund controlled by recipients attracts money at a different rate than a global fund they have to petition. The arithmetic is unforgiving: five donors and the host announced new money in one week at a venue the region itself convened, and the total moved by roughly ten million dollars.

Whether US$1 million is the going rate for Dutch climate-security and climate-resilience money, or a floor the Netherlands happened to set at one venue. The pledge to the Pacific fund on 7 to 9 October was the smallest of five made that week and two tenths of one per cent of that fund's initial target. Read it against the two other Dutch data points this digest holds: a €5 million structural defence climate line whose action plan is overdue, and the absence of the Netherlands from the fourteen governments funding the UN's joint climate-security programme. The same question was asked of Britain's £1 million three weeks ago and the answer there turned on the denominator. Here there is no favourable denominator available.

open_moves.text: Denmark's Security Council food-security debate, outcome document unconfirmed. Unchanged, and October is now closed as a route: the Council monitor's own forecast for the month carries no food-security item in any framing, under a presidency that named the succession as its substantive business. The next plausible venue is the joint seminar with the African Union on 21 and 22 October, where a food-security framing would be the African Union's to bring rather than a Council member's.

The American climate-security institute's philanthropic-funding bet. Advanced on register for a third consecutive week and the direction is now unmistakable. In the week to 11 October the institute published no climate research — a September media round-up and an event recap of New York Climate Week — while the parent organisation opened applications for a second cohort of a fellowship on artificial intelligence and national security, due 20 October. Three weeks without a state-level briefer. A philanthropically funded institute follows the money that is available, and the money that is available is on convergence with artificial intelligence.

The Abyei climate, peace and security report and the next peacekeeping mandate renewal. Unchanged, with one correction to this digest's own record of the Stockholm institute's output: the Lake Chad climate, peace and security fact sheet carried here as undated is dated June 2026. The climate-change-and-security publications list still ends at the August Abyei study, with nothing for September or October, which under this digest's split rule is lead time from a research institute and not a finding. The Abyei mandate and the Council's Africa items in late October are where this resolves.
PIF security-declaration merger.

The European integrated framework for climate resilience. Still 28 October, and this week revealed the strategy it belongs to. A draft of the Union's negotiating position for the November conference is reported to rule out new climate finance commitments; the framework is reported to arrive with a 3°C reference trajectory, named risk owners, member-state resilience plans conditioning access to Union funding, and an insurance architecture. Taken together that is a decision to manage climate risk by allocation at home rather than by transfer abroad. The parliament's own research service frames the package in security terms while the European Council three days earlier discusses defence without it. Note the date has already moved once, from 20 to 28 October.

Succession to the Secretary-General. Advanced and eroding. A fifth straw poll on 7 October with the same seven candidates and none withdrawn: the leader down from ten encourage to nine with six discourage, the second-placed candidate down from eight encourage to six, and the Guyanese candidate at her worst of the five. Four of seven lost ground. A sixth poll is set for 16 October and Council diplomats say it may be colour-coded to show whether the discouragement sits with a permanent member. The incumbent's term ends on 31 December. For this field the finding is unchanged through five polls: nobody has asked any candidate a public question about climate or about Council competence over it.

The November conference of the parties at Antalya, 9 to 20 November, under a Türkiye-Australia presidency. Advanced sharply and in a direction this digest did not expect. At the close of the preparatory talks on 8 October the president-designate priced the climate finance ask against the alliance's 5 per cent of national output defence commitment — "what does it mean to spend 5% for defense if you don't have a country to live on?" — which is recorded as its own move this week. He and the president of negotiations visited Tuvalu on 6 October with the heads of the Asian Development Bank and the Green Climate Fund. The contested division of labour is unresolved and now consequential: a presidency that disagrees with itself in public, arriving at a conference the Union has pre-emptively declared closed to new finance.

Whether overshoot is adopted as a planning premise by security institutions or stays inside the climate-policy system. Advanced again, and the adopting party this week is the one with most to lose by it: the Pacific's own preparatory meeting worked on limiting the overshoot of 1.5°C as an agenda item in its own right. Within six weeks the premise has been published by a UN agency, built into a European legislative proposal as a 3°C reference trajectory, and taken up as a work item by the small-island constituency that refused it in September. No security institution has adopted it, which is the original question and still unanswered.

Whether the small island states' legal-character defence of 1.5°C holds through the Assembly session and the November conference. Effectively superseded, and the supersession is the finding. The position at the preparatory talks was carried by Fiji rather than by the alliance, and what it defended was finance access and the ocean rather than the threshold's legal character; the meeting's own work item was limiting overshoot. The alliance's own pages were not tried this week. Treat the legal-character defence as not currently being prosecuted by anyone, rather than as defeated.

Whether the pre-event-indications finding produces a funded glacier-hazard early-warning programme, and whether it can survive the China-Nepal data wall. No movement. The bilateral mechanism that would have to carry the data question is two months past a commitment to meet, and Nepal's proposal for a regional mechanism is three weeks unanswered. Nothing from the mountain research centre this week.

Whether Nepal's restriction of foreign search-and-rescue becomes a precedent or an episode. Superseded in practice and worth closing soon. Nepal's posture is unambiguously outward-facing: a sovereign claim to a multilateral fund, a regional mechanism proposed from the Assembly rostrum, a reconstruction argument going to the lenders in Bangkok, and a draft national policy drafted with development-bank consultants. One new wrinkle on the capacity question: about 112 of some 1,453 recovered bodies had been identified, which says more about the limits of the response than the assistance restriction ever did.

Whether the climate convention secretariat's economic-security framing is picked up outside the climate-policy system, and in particular whether any European security institution adopts the formulation.
open_moves.resolution: Answered on both halves and not in the way the question expected. A European security institution did adopt a security framing: on 24 September the Union's High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy co-hosted a foreign ministers' dialogue on climate change and ecosystem degradation as national security risks. But it adopted this field's own formulation, national security risk, not the secretariat's economic-security substitution. And the secretary himself substituted again in the same week, telling Climate Week that electrification shields countries, families and businesses from fossil-fuel supply shocks and calling it a development strategy, an industrial strategy, a health strategy and a security strategy — security fourth, and meaning supply security. So the two moved past each other: the institution reached for the field's register in the same week the secretariat reached past it. The question is closed because its premise has been falsified. It assumed the secretariat's phrasing would be the vector by which the security frame travelled into European institutions, and the frame travelled without it.

open_moves.text: Whether the deltacommissaris's two-per-cent ask converts into any government commitment. Fourth checkpoint passed with silence: no cabinet response to the 2027 programme and nothing on water in the responsible committee. The nearest pressure is still external and now a fortnight off — the European framework of 28 October is expected to require named risk owners, which is awkward for a governance model built on distributed responsibility.

Whether Nepal's reconstruction bill produces a loss and damage response, and on what evidentiary basis. Unmoved for a sixth week and now fully dated. The ministers wrote on 31 August; board members from the African, Asia-Pacific and least-developed-country constituencies asked for an extraordinary meeting on 2 September; the co-chairs replied on 9 September that options must stay inside existing mandates and procedures; developed-country members backed an urgent consultation on 14 September; nothing since, and the board may not decide before or during the November conference. The separate US$20 million approved under the fund's Barbados modalities is on earlier proposals and is not this request. The fund's own site has still not opened for this routine.
Whether the rescission was announced as expected, whether the endangerment-finding proposal followed, and whether the Houston ministerial's outcome document mentions climate.
open_moves.resolution: All three answered. The partial repeal of the carbon pollution standards for fossil-fuel-fired power plants was finalised on 14 September 2026 by Administrator Lee Zeldin, signed at the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial in Houston rather than on its sidelines; the agency prices it at $310 billion in savings and calls it the largest power-sector deregulatory action in US history. The separate proposal followed simultaneously: EPA proposed rescinding every remaining greenhouse-gas standard for the sector, the vehicle for repealing the power-plant endangerment finding, with $370 million in claimed direct compliance-cost savings. And the ministerial's outcome document, a Critical Minerals Meeting Communiqué, does not mention climate: it grounds critical minerals in energy security, digital infrastructure, emerging technologies and economic development, and calls for voluntary and collaborative cooperation respecting national sovereignty and 'different domestic pathways'. Canada's own readout of the meeting likewise contains no reference to climate change. Environmental organisations have said they will litigate. The substitution this digest read off the ministerial's branding last week is confirmed in a negotiated multilateral text, which is why this closes as landed rather than as too early.

open_moves.text: Whether NATO ever states what happened to the Secretary-General's annual climate and security assessment. Still no statement. The centre of excellence welcomed its 2026 fellows on 6 October and publishes nothing; its Montréal summit on 15 and 16 October is the next dated observable and the test of whether the referent's removal from binding texts is a drafting discipline or a position.

Whether the relocation of the evidentiary question from causation to adaptation limits is taken up by the institutions that have to apply it. No fund board, bank, insurer or court reasoned from adaptation limits this week, three weeks after the study. The attribution network has published nothing since 17 September, including nothing on the Horn of Africa forecast and nothing on Europe's heat season — which, under this digest's split rule, is lead time from a research network and evidence about nothing. The only new route remains the European framework's named risk owners.

Whether the American climate-security field's move to the state level is a durable relocation or a holding pattern. Third consecutive week of counter-evidence and the question should probably be closed as answered no. No new state briefer since 18 September; no state government named as commissioner or partner on any of the five; no second American institute writing for statehouses; and the institute's parent spending its new programme capacity on an artificial-intelligence and national-security fellowship. The statehouse series was one bet among several and it is not the one being pressed.

Whether the asymmetry in the Dutch budget — flood defence funded, spatial adaptation and freshwater reduced over the longer term — survives the cabinet's response to the 2027 delta programme and the autumn estimates. No amendment and no cabinet response found; the parliamentary budget rounds on infrastructure and water fall later in the autumn, so this is lead time. The defence side of the same pattern hardened again: the €5 million structural climate-security line stands and the action plan that would spend it is now three months and one week overdue.

The British, European and Kenyan foreign ministers' dialogue on climate change and ecosystem degradation as national security risks, 24 September. Six weeks on, no institutional follow-through from any of the three, and nothing from the Union's external action service. The nearest thing in this week's record is a different capital's conference: the German foreign ministry's eighth annual climate-security convening on 6 October, which named existing instruments rather than new ones. One British follow-on that is money rather than machinery: £10 million to the Pacific's climate fund on 7 October, announced by its climate special representative.

Britain's £331 million for climate-driven instability, of which £330 million to the Global Environment Facility and £1 million to the joint United Nations climate security unit. Recalibrated again, and in Britain's favour. Two weeks after the package, the United Kingdom put £10 million into the Pacific Islands Forum's own climate fund on 7 October, announced by its climate special representative Rachael Kyte — ten times the climate-security unit allocation, into an instrument the recipients control, at the venue the recipients convened. So the £1 million was not the going rate for British climate money; it was the going rate for multilateral climate-security machinery specifically, which is a narrower and more interesting finding. The question now is why those two numbers differ by an order of magnitude.

Nepal's proposal, from the General Assembly rostrum on 24 September, for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by Nepal, India and China. Third week, no response from either capital, and the bilateral mechanism it would build on is two months past its own commitment to meet. Nepali commentary has started reframing it as a risk-intelligence system, which is what an unanswered diplomatic proposal becomes: a domestic capability argument.

NATO's revision and first public release of its seven baseline requirements for resilience, 15 September. Nothing new from the alliance. The dated observable is now four days out: the Montréal summit of 15 and 16 October, convened by the alliance's own climate change and security centre of excellence with a Canadian defence association, titled around climate-smart investment on the road to 5 per cent, with a Nordic resilience and infrastructure workshop on 14 October alongside it.

Australia's Climate Week keynote on climate security as national security, 21 September, and the challenge to it from a former chief of defence asking where the plan is. The near-term test has been answered, negatively. Australia's climate minister co-hosted and funded the preparatory talks he will preside over in November, and no security content appeared in what he presided over: the agenda was ocean, overshoot and finance access, and his own contribution was the distributional point that the countries needing finance most get it least. A good sentence, and not a security argument. Keynote and chairmanship remain separate registers for the same minister.

Fiji's four-pillar position for the pre-conference talks, set out on 29 September. Resolved in part, and recorded again as a move this week. The finance and ocean pillars landed: a pledging round took the region's own fund to about US$190 million and the ocean-climate nexus became a work item. The science pillar did not get transacted — no outcome language naming the climate panel as the reference science could be found — which is consistent with this week's correction, because the pillar was aimed at a substitution nobody is attempting while the real decision sat in a scientific-governance plenary four days later. Pacific leadership was demonstrated by the hosting.

The American climate-security institute's private tabletop exercise with a solar-geoengineering research organisation on the security dynamics of a fictional 2030 stratospheric aerosol injection deployment, 14 October, alongside the Montréal defence-climate summit, with no participants named and no output document. Unchanged and now part of a pair. On 6 October a foreign ministry put solar geoengineering on its annual climate-security conference programme for the first time, on the record. The same subject in the same fortnight in two formats, one of which produces a record and one of which is designed not to. Watch for any acknowledgement after 16 October, and for whether any state or alliance body is revealed to have taken part.

Greece's Security Council programme of work for October, announced 1 October. Confirmed against the Council monitor's own forecast rather than against the presidency's announcement, which is the stronger source: mandate renewals for the western Sahara mission, Libya, Colombia and the Bosnia force, all expiring 31 October; a children and armed conflict briefing chaired by the foreign minister; a high-level briefing on emerging technologies and maritime security; open debates on the Middle East and on women, peace and security; a joint seminar with the African Union on 21 and 22 October; and no climate, water, food-security or environment item in any framing. Resolves on 31 October, and the African Union item is the only remaining route.

The Berlin climate and security conference of 6 October 2026, hosted by the German foreign ministry with the institute that founded it in 2019. Held, and recorded as this week's first move. The foreign minister opened it by arguing that actors are using the impacts of climate change as a weapon, put the Group of Friends on Climate and Security at 81 members, and said solar geoengineering was on the programme for the first time; climate-resilient reconstruction in Syria was discussed with Syrian representatives present. No new money and no new machinery was announced, and there is still no standing output document, which is why eight editions have produced influence nobody can trace. Open on the only question the format leaves: whether any defence ministry repeats the weaponisation claim.

The November conference presidency's pricing of the climate finance ask against the alliance's 5 per cent of national output defence commitment, stated to reporters at Nadi on 8 October by Türkiye's environment minister and president-designate. Open on whether anyone takes the comparison up, and on which side it is taken up. The argument's strength is that it is from demonstrated political capacity rather than from threat: five per cent was found, so the money exists. Its risk is that a defence benchmark invites the answer that climate spending should come out of the 1.5 points of defence- and security-related expenditure — which is exactly what the alliance's own centre of excellence is convening a summit about on 15 and 16 October, and what the military council argued a year ago before going silent for twelve months. Resolves partly at Antalya in November, and partly in Montréal next week.

The Union's draft negotiating position for the November conference, reported on 6 October from a copy seen by a financial wire, stating there is no scope for new climate finance commitments and emphasising implementation of existing decisions, an extension of the mitigation work programme to at least 2040, and setting up the 2028 stocktake. Open on whether the phrase survives into the conclusions environment ministers were to approve on 12 October, and on whether the mitigation work programme extension is what it is traded for. Read it with the resilience framework of 28 October rather than alone: taken together they describe a bloc managing climate risk by domestic allocation and insurance rather than by international transfer, which is a coherent strategy and the first clear answer this digest has to the question of which register European climate policy is actually written in.
